statement: As described in the US Surgeon General's 2014 report (a narrative review with no stated search method; its figures are second-hand here), the burden of death and disease from tobacco in the United States is overwhelmingly caused by cigarettes and other combusted tobacco products; the report states this as a conclusion about products and does not divide the harm between nicotine and the other substances in smoke. For nicotine on its own, compared with burning tobacco and with no tobacco use, its chapter on nicotine grades six conclusions. Sufficient to infer a causal relationship: nicotine is acutely toxic at high enough doses (drawn from animal studies, medicine trials and poisoning reports, with no systematic dose-response assessment); nicotine activates biological pathways through which smoking raises the risk of disease (experimental research); nicotine exposure in the fetus has lasting adverse effects on brain development (the chapter's support is brief and experimental, with a pointer to a later chapter that was not read; it describes no human study that separates nicotine from the rest of the smoke); and nicotine adversely affects maternal and fetal health in pregnancy, contributing to preterm delivery and stillbirth (inferred from studies of smokeless tobacco in Sweden and India, trials of nicotine replacement in pregnancy and experiments; for example Swedish snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.43, smaller than for smoking (the report's printed figure for smoking is a misprint and is not quoted), and, in a trial of 250 pregnant women, higher birth weight in the nicotine-patch group than in the placebo group, 186 g, 95% CI 35 to 336, with no difference in quit rates, possibly because of less smoking; the chapter reads the studies together as supporting a modest role for nicotine in fetal growth restriction). Outside its graded conclusions, the chapter's summary says animal studies, including in primates, consistently show that nicotine may be the primary mediator of many of the adverse effects of maternal smoking on fetal lung development. Suggestive but not sufficient: nicotine exposure in adolescence may have lasting adverse effects on brain development (smoking in adolescence is linked to lasting cognitive and behavioural problems, but confounding makes cause hard to establish). Inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship: nicotine and cancer (genotoxicity data are mixed; animal studies mostly do not show nicotine alone to cause tumours; the one human follow-up of people who used nicotine replacement long term, a short one, had 75 lung cancers among 3,220 people followed for 7 more years, with no link to replacement use; at least some forms of smokeless tobacco raise the risk of cancers of the mouth, oesophagus and pancreas, by less than smoking and without raising many smoking-related cancers, which the chapter reads as suggesting nicotine may not be a strong tumour promoter in people, while cautioning that oral and inhaled exposure differ). The chapter has no numbered conclusion on the heart (its text says it is likely that nicotine's effects on heart rate, heart contraction, resistance in the coronary vessels and insulin sensitivity contribute to some extent to the cardiovascular risk of people who smoke) or on dependence (it carries earlier reports forward: nicotine is the major chemical in tobacco responsible for dependence, the risk depends on how fast and how much nicotine is delivered, not all forms of nicotine delivery carry the same risk of dependence, nicotine replacement medicines designed to minimise it carry a low risk, and cigarettes have been designed to raise the likelihood of dependence through contents and emissions beyond nicotine). It also reports modest thinking-enhancing effects of acute nicotine in adults who smoke during withdrawal (and, in its evidence summary, in adults who do not smoke), with little known about long-term effects; that authors with industry funding reported positive findings on nicotine and thinking almost exclusively, as cited; that the long-term effects of nicotine, compared with smoking and with no tobacco use, still need study; and that all tobacco products contain toxicants and so carry some health risk. Not measured: the share of smoking's harm that is due to nicotine, and long-term outcomes in people who use nicotine without smoke. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
population: People and laboratory animals exposed to nicotine on its own (as medicine, in smokeless tobacco or in experiments), and people who smoke, as reviewed in the US Surgeon General's 2014 report
exposure: Nicotine on its own, without the other substances in tobacco smoke
comparator: Burning tobacco (cigarette smoke), and no tobacco or nicotine use
outcome: Acute poisoning; disease-related biological pathways; fetal brain and lung development and pregnancy outcomes; adolescent brain development; cancer; heart disease; dependence; each as graded or described by the report
magnitude: No effect size is given for most conclusions. Where cited: Swedish population study 1999 to 2010, snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.43), smaller than for smoking (the smoking figure is printed as 2.27 with an interval of 2.62 to 2.91, a misprint because the estimate lies outside its own interval, so it is not quoted); preterm delivery 27% higher with smoking (Shah and Bracken 2000, as cited), with a rise of similar size for snus in Sweden; trial of nicotine patches in 250 pregnant women: birth weight 186 g higher (35 to 336), no difference in quit rates; Lung Health Study: 5,887 enrolled, 3,220 followed for 7 more years, 75 lung cancers, no link with nicotine replacement use. Grades: sufficient for 4 conclusions, suggestive but not sufficient for 1, inadequate for 1. The report apportions none of the harm between nicotine and smoke.

evidence.extracted: States that the burden of death and disease from tobacco use in the United States is overwhelmingly caused by cigarettes and other combusted tobacco products and that rapid elimination of their use would dramatically reduce it. It is a statement about products; the report does not divide the burden between nicotine and the other constituents of smoke.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Conclusions, conclusions 1 to 6; Chapter 1 › Chapter Conclusions › Chapter 5
evidence.extracted: The six graded conclusions of the nicotine chapter: sufficient to infer that at high enough doses nicotine has acute toxicity (1); that nicotine activates multiple biological pathways through which smoking increases the risk of disease (2); that nicotine exposure during fetal development has lasting adverse consequences for brain development (3); that nicotine adversely affects maternal and fetal health in pregnancy, contributing to adverse outcomes such as preterm delivery and stillbirth (4). Suggestive, not sufficient, that exposure during adolescence may have lasting adverse consequences for brain development (5). Inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship between nicotine and cancer risk (6).

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Toxicokinetics and Acute Toxicity of Nicotine › Acute Toxicity of Nicotine, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (the 3rd follows Table 5.1); Summary, 1st paragraph; Evidence Summary, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Acute toxicity data on nicotine are limited and come from three sources: animal studies, trials of nicotine as a medicine and poisoning reports. The animal studies do not adequately characterize acute toxicity; the medicine trials use amounts chosen because they are thought to be subtoxic; poisonings are documented, but the literature has not been assessed systematically for the relation between amount and effect; the commonly quoted human fatal oral amount is poorly documented (the chapter's literature search found no source for it). The Summary says nicotine has known acute toxicity and that poisoning is possible from ingesting nicotine-containing products. No amounts are used in this claim.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure › Reproductive Health Outcomes, 3rd paragraph; Fetal Growth Restriction, 1st paragraph; Preterm Delivery, 1st paragraph; Stillbirth, Perinatal Mortality, and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome, 1st paragraph; Summary, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Inference about nicotine alone in pregnancy comes from studies comparing prenatal smokeless tobacco with prenatal smoking (smokeless products do not expose people to combustion products but all contain nicotine; Swedish snus has lower levels of some toxicants) and from randomized trials of nicotine therapy in pregnant women. Fetal growth: smokeless tobacco shows only modest contributions to lower birth weight; Swedish population study 1999 to 2010, snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.43), smaller than for smoking (the smoking figure is printed as 2.27 with an interval of 2.62 to 2.91, so it is not quoted); a trial of 250 pregnant women found no difference in quit rates or saliva cotinine between nicotine-patch and placebo arms but a birth weight 186 g higher (35 to 336) in the patch arm, possibly due to less smoking; the chapter reads these as supporting a modest role for nicotine in fetal growth restriction. Preterm delivery: smoking linked to a 27% higher risk (Shah and Bracken 2000, as cited); rises of similar size with snus and with smoking in Sweden. Stillbirth: higher risk with smokeless tobacco in India and Sweden; in the Swedish study the smoking-related stillbirth risk fell markedly when antenatal bleeding and small-for-gestational-age deliveries were excluded while the snus risk stayed the same, which the chapter reads as both involving nicotine, with other factors also contributing in smoking. Summary: the evidence supports a key role for nicotine in the adverse effects of smoking on reproductive health, including preterm delivery and stillbirth.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure › Cognitive Function › Critical Periods of Exposure in the Nervous System, 1st paragraph; Cognitive Function › Summary, 1st paragraph; Lung Development › Summary, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Fetal brain: nicotine targets neurotransmitter receptors in the fetal brain and may alter cell proliferation and synaptic activity (one cited review); the effects of prenatal exposure on the nervous system are referred to chapter 9 (not read); the cognitive function summary says evidence shows adverse effects of cigarette smoke and of nicotine on fetal and adolescent brain development. No human study that separates nicotine from the rest of the smoke is described in the sections read. Lung: primate and other animal studies consistently suggest nicotine may be the primary mediator of many of the adverse effects of maternal smoking on fetal lung development.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure › Cognitive Function › Critical Periods of Exposure in the Nervous System, 3rd, 4th, 8th and 9th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Smoking in adolescence is associated with lasting cognitive and behavioural impairments, including effects on working memory and attention, but causal relationships are hard to establish with potential confounding; animal studies show that nicotine in adolescence affects the brain differently from exposure at other ages; the concluding paragraph calls adverse effects of adolescent exposure on cognition likely, while the graded conclusion is only suggestive (the graded level is used here); effects after adolescence and young adulthood are unknown.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure › Cancer › Genotoxicity, 1st paragraph; Experimental Animal Studies for Carcinogenicity, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Human Studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Summary, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Genotoxicity data are mixed (most assays negative, two positive). Animal studies mostly do not show nicotine alone to be tumour-causing (one exception: sarcomas in one mouse strain); nicotine promotes tumours in some models but not those driven by tobacco-specific nitrosamines; the animal findings do not support nicotine as a complete carcinogen. People: very little data; the Lung Health Study is the only source on long-term nicotine replacement (5,887 enrolled, 3,220 followed 7 more years, 75 lung cancers, no link with replacement use; short follow-up); smokeless tobacco raises the risk of cancers of the mouth, oesophagus and pancreas, less than smoking, and does not raise many smoking-related cancers, which suggests nicotine may not have a strong tumour-promoting effect, tempered by the different route (oral rather than inhaled). Summary: insufficient data to conclude that nicotine causes or contributes to cancer in humans; possible oral, oesophageal and pancreatic risks; substantial experimental evidence that nicotine is active in carcinogenic mechanisms; in vitro data suggestive but not supported overall by the most recent animal studies.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure › Cardiovascular Diseases, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The chapter says it is likely that the sympathomimetic effects of nicotine (faster heart rate, stronger heart contraction, higher coronary vascular resistance, lower insulin sensitivity) contribute to some extent to cardiovascular risk in people who smoke; other mechanisms are proposed (for example atherosclerosis in a mouse model); a gene-cluster association with peripheral arterial disease cannot separate a direct role of nicotine from the level of dependence. There is no numbered conclusion on the heart in chapter 5.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Introduction, 1st paragraph; Toxicokinetics and Acute Toxicity of Nicotine, 1st paragraph; Pathophysiology of Nicotine Addiction › Summary of Evidence from the 2010 Surgeon General's Report, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The 1988 report concluded that nicotine is the drug in tobacco that causes dependence; the chapter calls nicotine the major chemical component responsible for dependence in tobacco products; the risk depends on the amount of nicotine delivered and the way it is delivered, and the potential for dependence rises with the rate of delivery, the rate of absorption and the concentration reached; not all forms of nicotine delivery pose an equal risk of establishing or maintaining dependence; nicotine replacement medicines designed to minimise the risk carry a low risk and are generally much easier to stop than tobacco products; cigarettes are engineered to raise the likelihood of dependence through contents and emissions beyond nicotine and through design features. Chapter 5 has no 2014 conclusion of its own on dependence.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure › Cognitive Function › Effects of Nicotine on Cognitive Function in Healthy Adult Smokers and Nonsmokers, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Tobacco Industry Influence, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Evidence Summary, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Implications, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Acute nicotine has modest cognition-enhancing effects in adults who smoke during withdrawal (the evidence summary adds adults who do not smoke); a meta-analysis of double-blind placebo-controlled studies (nicotine given mainly as replacement products) found enhancement in 6 of 9 performance domains in people who do not smoke and in people who smoke and had been abstinent for up to 2 hours; less is known about long-term exposure. The chapter reports that a 1997 review found authors acknowledging industry funding reported positive findings on nicotine and cognitive performance almost exclusively while authors without industry funding reported positive and negative findings, that in studies of smoking and Alzheimer's disease the pooled odds ratios without industry funding were neutral or showed higher risk with smoking while industry-affiliated studies showed lower risk, and that industry ties are often not disclosed in articles citing such work. The report calls for information on the risks of long-term nicotine exposure compared with smoking and with no tobacco use at all, says long-term nicotine use may have adverse consequences for those exposed and harms the developing fetus, names cancer, cardiovascular and neurocognitive outcomes as of concern, and states that all tobacco products contain toxicants and so all tobacco product use poses some health risks.

evidence.locator: Chapter 3 › Methods for Reviewing the Evidence and Developing Conclusions; Chapter 1 › Table 1.1; Development of the Report
evidence.extracted: Grading in the report: four levels from a synthesis of all the evidence, using consistency, strength, specificity, temporality and coherence; meta-analytic significance has not figured directly in its causal inferences; conclusions are worded conservatively; no databases, dates or selection rules are described for the conclusions used, so the report is read as a narrative review.

risk_of_bias.note: Narrative review: no databases, dates or selection rules are stated for the conclusions used, the cited studies are not appraised with a tool, the supporting text for the fetal brain conclusion is brief, and the chapter text calls adolescent effects likely while its graded conclusion is only suggestive.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: the report states where results are mixed (for example genotoxicity assays) and grades the cancer question inadequate.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: none of the cited studies was read. Evidence on nicotine on its own in people is indirect: experiments in animals and cells, trials of medicines, and smokeless tobacco such as snus, which also contains other substances; the one long-term human follow-up of nicotine replacement was short.

imprecision.note: No estimate is claimed beyond the figures the report cites.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the report notes that authors with industry funding reported positive findings on nicotine and thinking almost exclusively.

grade.reasoning: A description of what a narrative review concluded, seen only through that review. Observational and experimental evidence starts low (METHODS 6.3) and a claim seen only through reviews is downgraded for risk of bias (not appraisable: no search method, cited studies not appraised) and for indirectness (second-hand; nicotine on its own in people is mostly inferred from other products and from animals): very low, the floor. The relation is 'describes' because the claim reports the report's graded conclusions and not an effect of nicotine measured by the editors; the grades (sufficient, suggestive, inadequate) are the authors' judgments. Major Conclusion 9 is read as a statement about which products cause the burden, not as showing how much of the harm is due to smoke rather than nicotine, which the report does not apportion. Status single study: one report is the source and its figures come from primary studies that were not read. It stays draft because it rests only on a narrative review (METHODS 6.3 and 12).

verification.flag_note: Draft for section 7 by the co-editor (decision p-ways-of-taking): held off the site until the senior author approves this version. Rests only on the 2014 report (chapter 1 listings, chapter 5 and chapter 3 on grading), a narrative review, so it stays draft (METHODS 6.3). Not read: chapters 2, 4 and 6 to 15 (among them chapter 9, which chapter 5 cites for the fetal nervous system and whose own text on it is brief) and every cited study. The cigarette odds ratio printed with an interval that excludes it (2.27, interval 2.62 to 2.91) is not quoted; the primary Swedish study (Baba et al. 2013, as cited) has no reference record. Amounts given in the toxicity section and in the pregnancy trial are deliberately left out. The report's call for cautious messages to some groups is not used (advice stays with the senior author).
